Mathematicians prove decades-old conjecture about prime gaps

Published 2026-10-07 11:30 UTC

For more than half a century, mathematicians have tried to understand how far apart consecutive prime numbers can be. Primes become rarer as numbers grow, so the gaps between them tend to widen, but the pattern is irregular: twin primes sit just two apart, while some stretches of numbers contain no primes for a long time.

Now a team of three number theorists has proved a decades-old conjecture that places a new upper bound on those gaps. Their result shows that, beyond a certain point, the gap between a prime and the next one is always smaller than a specific power of the first prime, improving on a bound that had stood since the 1970s.

The proof combines two older techniques in a new way. One is a sieve method, which counts numbers that avoid being divisible by small primes. The other comes from harmonic analysis and studies how primes are distributed in arithmetic progressions. By carefully balancing errors in each method, the authors squeezed out enough precision to close the remaining gap in the argument.

Other mathematicians described the work as technically impressive. One researcher who was not involved said the key innovation is a lemma that controls rare configurations of primes that had blocked earlier attempts. The paper runs to more than 80 pages and has been checked by several groups since it appeared online in the spring.

The result does not settle the most famous questions about primes, such as whether there are infinitely many twin primes. But it sharpens the picture of how primes are spread out, and experts expect the new lemma to find uses in other problems.

The authors say they began the project during a summer workshop, sketching ideas on a whiteboard. It took four years to turn the sketch into a complete proof.
